title: Radio, Television, the Clip
bigQuestion: How did radio, television and the short clip change what people know and remember about sport?

story.title: Five Seconds in Salt Lake City
story.kicker: A whole championship game shrinks to one shot that plays again and again.
paragraphs: On June 14, 1998, the Chicago Bulls played the Utah Jazz in Game 6 of the NBA Finals. The game was in the Delta Center in Salt Lake City, more than 1,200 miles from Chicago. Millions of people in the Chicago area watched it on television. Bars, kitchens and living rooms across the city tuned to the same broadcast.

The game lasted about two and a half hours on the clock of a real evening. Scottie Pippen, the Bulls' second star, played through painful back spasms. The lead changed hands again and again. Utah led by three points with less than a minute to play.

Then Michael Jordan scored, stole the ball from Karl Malone, and made a jump shot with 5.2 seconds left. The Bulls won 87 to 86. Jordan finished with 45 points. The win gave Chicago its sixth NBA title in eight seasons.

Within hours, the last shot played on news shows across the country. In later years it appeared in advertisements, documentaries and endless online videos. Many fans who were not yet born in 1998 can describe that one shot. Far fewer can name anything else that happened in the game.

A grandfather in Chicago might remember the whole night: Pippen limping, the long wait, the nervous final minutes. His granddaughter may know only the five seconds she has seen on a phone. Both are real memories. They were shaped by different kinds of media.
story.think: What does a short clip keep, and what does it leave out, compared with watching the whole game?

lessons.title: Wires and Box Scores
lessons.mainIdea: Before radio, fans followed distant games through telegraph reports and printed box scores in newspapers and weekly sports papers.
reading: In the 1800s, the *telegraph* sent coded electric signals along wires from one city to another. Newspapers used it to receive scores from games far away. By the late 1800s, a game played in one city could be reported in another city's paper the next morning. Crowds sometimes stood outside newspaper offices, where workers posted scores on a board as each report arrived.

Henry Chadwick shaped how baseball was written down. He was born in England in 1824 and came to the United States as a boy. He wrote about baseball for New York newspapers for decades. He is often credited with developing the *box score*, a small table that lists each player's times at bat, runs and hits. The Baseball Hall of Fame honored him in 1938.

Weekly papers carried these numbers across the country. *The Sporting News* began in St. Louis in 1886. It printed box scores, standings and averages, and people nicknamed it "the Bible of Baseball." A fan in a small town could follow a big-city team week by week. What that fan knew came as numbers and printed words, not as sounds or pictures.

words.d: a system that sent coded electric signals along wires to carry messages between places
a printed table that sums up a game with each player's numbers
a weekly sports paper founded in St. Louis in 1886, known for baseball coverage

look.title: Reading an Old Box Score
look.text: Picture a newspaper page from 1900. Under a headline sits a narrow block of names and numbers. Each row is a player. The columns show times at bat, runs and hits. The block does not say whether it rained, how big the crowd was, or who argued with the umpire.
look.prompt: What can a reader learn from a box score, and what can a reader not learn from it?

check.q: What did the telegraph let newspapers do?
choices: receive scores from games in other cities
check.why: The telegraph sent coded signals along wires, so papers could get scores from far away.

check.q: Which writer is often credited with developing the baseball box score?
check.why: Henry Chadwick, a New York baseball writer born in 1824, is often credited with the box score.

check.q: Where and when did The Sporting News begin?
check.why: The Sporting News began in St. Louis in 1886.

lessons.title: Radio Reaches the Ballpark
lessons.mainIdea: In 1920 and 1921, radio stations began carrying news and then live play-by-play of baseball games into homes.
reading: On November 2, 1920, station KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcast the results of the presidential election. The Westinghouse company owned the station. KDKA is often called one of the first commercial radio stations in the United States. A *broadcast* is a program sent out by radio or television for anyone with a receiver to hear or see.

On August 5, 1921, KDKA announcer Harold Arlin described a game between the Pittsburgh Pirates and the Philadelphia Phillies at Forbes Field. It is widely called the first major league game carried on radio. This kind of live report, telling each event as it happens, is called *play-by-play*. That fall, reports from the World Series between the New York Giants and the New York Yankees also went out over the air.

Radio spread quickly through the 1920s. The 1930 census found that about 40 percent of American homes had a radio set. For the first time, a family could hear a game as it happened without a ticket. Team owners had to decide whether radio would build new fans or keep people away from the ballpark. That argument lasted for years.

words.d: a program sent out by radio or television for anyone with a receiver
a live report that describes each event of a game as it happens
a Pittsburgh radio station that began regular broadcasts in 1920

sections.title: Fights and Games on the Air

lessons.title: A Nation Listens to Boxing
lessons.mainIdea: Heavyweight fights of the 1920s were among the first events that huge audiences heard live on radio at the same moment.
reading: On July 2, 1921, a radio hookup carried the heavyweight fight between Jack Dempsey and Georges Carpentier from Jersey City, New Jersey. The Radio Corporation of America, or RCA, helped arrange it. Listeners gathered in theaters, clubs and halls with receivers. Many historians point to it as the first sports event that showed radio could draw a mass audience.

By 1927, stations could be linked into a *network*, a group of stations that share the same program at the same time. The National Broadcasting Company, or NBC, had formed in 1926. On September 22, 1927, NBC carried the second Dempsey and Gene Tunney fight from Soldier Field in Chicago. Announcer Graham McNamee described it to listeners across the country.

That Chicago fight is remembered for the "Long Count." After Tunney went down in the seventh round, the referee waited for Dempsey to go to a neutral corner before starting the count. Tunney got up and won the decision. Listeners could not see the delay. They argued about it using the words of the announcer and the newspaper stories that followed.

words.d: a group of radio or television stations that carry the same program at the same time
the National Broadcasting Company, a radio network formed in 1926
the name for the delayed count in the 1927 Dempsey and Tunney fight at Soldier Field

look.title: Hearing a Fight You Cannot See
look.text: It is September 22, 1927. A family in a small Iowa town sits close to a radio. They hear the crowd at Soldier Field roar. The announcer says Tunney is down. Seconds pass before the count begins. The family cannot see the ring or the referee. All they have is one man's voice.
look.prompt: How might the family's idea of the Long Count differ from the idea of a person sitting at ringside?

check.q: What is a broadcast network?
choices: a single station in one city
a group of stations carrying the same program at once
check.why: A network links many stations so they share one program at the same time, as NBC did from 1926.

check.q: Where was the 1927 Dempsey and Tunney fight held?
check.why: The Long Count fight took place at Soldier Field in Chicago on September 22, 1927.

check.q: Why could radio listeners not settle the Long Count argument themselves?
choices: They could only hear the announcer, not see the ring.
The count was printed in a box score.
check.why: Radio carried sound only, so listeners depended on the announcer's words.

lessons.title: Louis and Schmeling
lessons.mainIdea: The 1938 fight between Joe Louis and Max Schmeling was heard by a vast radio audience in the United States and Germany as a symbol before World War II.
reading: Joe Louis was born in Alabama in 1914 and grew up in Detroit. On June 19, 1936, he lost to Max Schmeling of Germany at Yankee Stadium. The Nazi government in Germany used Schmeling's win in its *propaganda*, which means messages meant to push a political idea. Nazi leaders claimed the result proved their false ideas about race.

On June 22, 1937, Louis beat James J. Braddock at Comiskey Park in Chicago to become heavyweight champion. He was the first Black heavyweight champion since Jack Johnson, who held the title from 1908 to 1915. Many Black newspapers, including the Chicago Defender, followed his career closely. For many Black Americans, his fights were shared public events.

The rematch with Schmeling came on June 22, 1938, at Yankee Stadium. Louis won by knockout in the first round, in about two minutes. Radio carried the fight across the United States and to Germany. Many accounts say the German broadcast went off the air before the finish. Louis's fast win was heard as a message about democracy and fascism, even though Schmeling himself did not choose that role.

words.d: messages spread to push a political idea, often by bending the truth
the boxing division for the heaviest fighters, with its own champion
a second contest between the same two opponents

look.title: Two Countries, One Radio Fight
look.text: On the night of June 22, 1938, people in American cities crowd around radios in homes, bars and barbershops. Across the ocean, German listeners hear the same fight on their own stations. In the United States the broadcast lasts to the end. Many accounts say the German broadcast went quiet before the finish. The next day, newspapers in each country explain the result in their own way.
look.prompt: Why might two countries describe the same fight in very different ways in 1938?

check.q: In which ballpark did Joe Louis become heavyweight champion in 1937?
check.why: Louis beat James J. Braddock at Comiskey Park in Chicago on June 22, 1937.

check.q: What does propaganda mean?
choices: messages spread to push a political idea
check.why: Propaganda is messaging meant to push a political idea; the Nazi government used Schmeling's 1936 win that way.

check.q: How did the 1938 rematch end?
choices: The fight was stopped by rain.
Louis won by knockout in the first round.
check.why: Louis knocked out Schmeling in the first round on June 22, 1938.

lessons.title: Games Rebuilt in a Studio
lessons.mainIdea: Early radio stations often re-created road games from telegraph reports, and team owners argued over whether radio helped or hurt ticket sales.
reading: Sending an announcer to every road game cost money. Many stations used a *re-creation* instead. An announcer sat in a studio and read short telegraph reports of each pitch. He added sound effects and described the game as if he were there. Before becoming an actor and later president, Ronald Reagan re-created Chicago Cubs games this way for station WHO in Des Moines, Iowa, in the 1930s.

Owners disagreed about radio. William Wrigley Jr., who owned the Cubs, let several Chicago stations carry his team's games in the 1920s. He believed radio would turn listeners into paying fans. Some other owners feared that free games on the air would empty their seats.

In New York, the Yankees, Giants and Dodgers agreed in the 1930s to keep their regular games off the radio. In 1939, Brooklyn Dodgers executive Larry MacPhail broke that agreement. He hired announcer Red Barber, who had worked for him in Cincinnati. The Dodgers' games went on the air, and the other New York clubs soon followed. Radio rights became a source of income for teams.

words.d: a radio broadcast built in a studio from telegraph reports, as if the announcer were at the game
the permission, usually sold by a team or league, to broadcast its games
a game a team plays in another team's city

look.title: A Studio in Des Moines
look.text: A young announcer sits at a desk in Iowa. A worker hands him a slip of paper from the telegraph. It gives the batter's name and a short code for what happened. The announcer turns those few words into a full scene: the crowd, the wind, the throw. The listeners hundreds of miles away hear a game that feels live.
look.prompt: Which parts of a re-created broadcast came from the game, and which parts came from the announcer?

check.q: What was a radio re-creation?
choices: a game rebuilt in a studio from telegraph reports
a second game played the next day
a film of a game shown in a theater
check.why: In a re-creation, an announcer in a studio turned telegraph reports into a live-sounding broadcast.

check.q: Which owner let Chicago stations carry Cubs games in the 1920s?
check.why: Cubs owner William Wrigley Jr. believed radio would build new fans.

check.q: What happened in 1939 in New York?
choices: The Dodgers began broadcasting games with Red Barber.
Radio was banned from all ballparks.
check.why: Larry MacPhail broke the New York clubs' radio agreement and hired Red Barber in 1939.

lessons.title: The First Cameras
lessons.mainIdea: Television began showing sport in the late 1930s, first to tiny audiences in Berlin and New York.
reading: The 1936 Summer Olympics in Berlin were shown on television, but few people saw them. Germany had very few home sets. The broadcasts went to public viewing rooms in and near Berlin. The Nazi government ran the Games as a show of national power, and the new pictures were part of that show.

In the United States, NBC ran an experimental television station in New York called W2XBS. On May 17, 1939, it televised a college baseball game between Columbia and Princeton at Baker Field, with Bill Stern announcing. It is generally called the first televised baseball game. The picture came from a single camera, so viewers often could not follow the ball.

On August 26, 1939, W2XBS showed a major league game for the first time. The Cincinnati Reds played the Brooklyn Dodgers at Ebbets Field, and Red Barber called it. Only a few hundred sets in the New York area could receive it. World War II then slowed the growth of *television* for several years.

words.d: a system that sends moving pictures and sound to a receiving set
a station allowed to test new technology before regular service
NBC's experimental New York television station of the 1930s

look.title: One Camera, One Ball
look.text: It is May 1939. A camera sits on a stand near home plate at Baker Field. It can show the pitcher and the batter. When the batter hits the ball, it flies out of the picture. The announcer must tell viewers where it went. Only a handful of people in New York are watching.
look.prompt: How did early television depend on the announcer, just as radio did?

check.q: Which game is generally called the first televised baseball game?
choices: Reds and Dodgers at Ebbets Field
Columbia and Princeton at Baker Field
Pirates and Phillies at Forbes Field
Giants and Yankees in the World Series
check.why: W2XBS showed Columbia and Princeton at Baker Field on May 17, 1939.

check.q: Why did few people see the 1936 Berlin Olympics on television?
choices: Germany had very few home sets, so viewing was in public rooms.
The Games were shown only on radio.
check.why: There were few home sets, so broadcasts went to public viewing rooms in and near Berlin.

check.q: Who called the first televised major league game in 1939?
check.why: Red Barber called the Reds and Dodgers game at Ebbets Field on August 26, 1939.

lessons.title: Sets Fill the Homes
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1950s, television spread to most American homes, and big games became shared national events.
reading: After World War II, factories built television sets in large numbers. In 1950, about 9 percent of American homes had a set. By 1960, about 87 percent did. In ten years, television went from a rare object to a normal piece of furniture. Watching a game no longer required a ticket, a bar or a neighbor.

Chicago had its own television stations early. WGN-TV went on the air in 1948 and carried Cubs games that year. For decades, Cubs home games played mostly in the afternoon at Wrigley Field, because the park had no lights until 1988. Families and students across the Midwest watched those day games on local television.

On December 28, 1958, the Baltimore Colts beat the New York Giants 23 to 17 in the NFL Championship Game at Yankee Stadium. It was the first NFL title game decided in *overtime*, extra play after a tied game. NBC carried it across the country. Writers soon called it "the Greatest Game Ever Played," and many historians say it helped make pro football a television sport.

words.d: extra play added when a game is tied at the end of regular time
a Chicago television station that began in 1948 and carried Cubs games
all the people who live together in one home

look.title: American Homes With a Television
look.cite: Nielsen household estimates, as summarized by the Television Bureau of Advertising
look.prompt: Between which two years did the share of homes with a television grow the most?

check.q: About what share of American homes had a television in 1960?
check.why: Television spread fast in the 1950s; by 1960 about 87 percent of homes had a set.

check.q: What does overtime mean?
choices: extra play after a tied game
check.why: Overtime is extra play; the 1958 NFL Championship was the first NFL title game decided that way.

check.q: Why did most Cubs home games stay in the afternoon for decades?
choices: Wrigley Field had no lights until 1988.
The team played in a dome.
check.why: Wrigley Field had no lights until 1988, so Cubs home games were day games.

lessons.title: One League, One Contract
lessons.mainIdea: A 1961 federal law let leagues sell television rights as a package, and national TV money reshaped pro football.
reading: In the 1950s, each NFL team sold its own television rights. Big-city teams earned much more than small-city teams. Pete Rozelle became NFL commissioner in 1960 and wanted the league to sell one national contract and share the money. A federal judge ruled that such a deal broke *antitrust* law, which forbids businesses from joining together to limit competition.

Congress answered with the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961. President John F. Kennedy signed it that September. The law allowed football, baseball, basketball and hockey leagues to pool their television rights and sell them together. The NFL signed a league-wide contract with CBS. Every team received an equal share, which helped small-market clubs like the Green Bay Packers compete.

Television money grew with the audience. The first AFL-NFL World Championship Game, later called Super Bowl I, was played on January 15, 1967, in Los Angeles. CBS and NBC both broadcast it. In 1970, ABC began Monday Night Football, putting a game in prime time, the evening hours when the most people watch. In 1973, Congress required that home games sold out 72 hours ahead be shown on local television.

words.d: laws that stop businesses from joining together to limit competition
a 1961 federal law letting leagues sell their television rights as one package
the evening hours when the largest number of people watch television
the top official who runs a sports league

look.title: The Sports Broadcasting Act
look.text: Antitrust laws shall not apply to an agreement among teams in a professional league of football, baseball, basketball or hockey to sell or transfer, as a group, their rights to televise the league's games.
look.cite: Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961, Public Law 87-331 (15 U.S.C. 1291)
look.prompt: What did this law allow leagues to do that a court had said they could not do?

check.q: What does antitrust law forbid?
choices: businesses joining together to limit competition
check.why: Antitrust laws stop businesses from teaming up to limit competition; a judge first ruled the NFL's pooled TV deal broke them.

check.q: What did the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 allow?
choices: leagues to sell television rights as one package

check.why: The 1961 law let leagues pool and sell their television rights together.

check.q: Which networks broadcast Super Bowl I in 1967?
check.why: Both CBS and NBC showed the first AFL-NFL World Championship Game on January 15, 1967.

lessons.title: Replay and the Highlight
lessons.mainIdea: Instant replay in 1963 and all-sports cable in 1979 turned games into short pieces that could be shown again and again.
reading: On December 7, 1963, CBS director Tony Verna used a new method during the Army and Navy football game in Philadelphia. He replayed a touchdown on videotape seconds after it happened. The announcer had to tell viewers it was not a second touchdown. This was the first *instant replay* on live American television.

Replay changed what a game was on the screen. One moment could now be shown several times, slowed down, or saved for later. ABC's Wide World of Sports, which began in 1961 under producer Roone Arledge, built whole programs from edited *highlights*. A highlight is a short piece of video that shows one important moment.

On September 7, 1979, ESPN began broadcasting from Bristol, Connecticut. Its first program was SportsCenter, a news show made largely of highlights. Cable television let the channel send sport around the clock. Fans who missed a game could see its biggest plays that night, in a minute or less. For many viewers, the highlight became the main way they knew a game.

words.d: showing a recorded moment again seconds after it happens during a live broadcast
short pieces of video showing the most important moments of a game
magnetic tape that records moving pictures and sound
an all-sports cable channel that began on September 7, 1979

look.title: From Replay to All-Day Sports

choices: 1963 at the Army and Navy game
check.why: Tony Verna of CBS used it during the Army and Navy game on December 7, 1963.

check.q: What is a highlight?
choices: a short video of one important moment
check.why: A highlight shows one key moment in a short clip.

check.q: What was ESPN's first program in 1979?
check.why: SportsCenter, a highlight and news show, was ESPN's first program.

lessons.title: The Catch Without the Game
lessons.mainIdea: Film and replay keep famous moments alive, but they can make people forget the rest of the game around them.
reading: On September 29, 1954, the New York Giants played the Cleveland Indians in Game 1 of the World Series at the Polo Grounds. In the eighth inning, with the score tied, Willie Mays ran down a long drive by Vic Wertz with his back to home plate. Film of that play has been shown for more than seventy years. It is known simply as "The Catch."

The rest of the game is far less remembered. It went to ten innings. Dusty Rhodes, a pinch hitter, won it for the Giants with a three-run home run. The Giants went on to sweep the series in four games. A fan who knows only the film might think the catch itself won the game.

Filmmakers helped shape which moments lasted. In 1962, Ed Sabol's small film company bought the rights to film the NFL championship game. The league bought his company in the mid-1960s and named it NFL Films. Its slow-motion shots, music and narration turned seasons into dramatic stories. Historians call this process *collective memory*: what a whole group remembers together, often shaped by the images it sees most.

words.d: what a whole group of people remembers together about the past
a baseball player sent in to bat in place of another player
the league-owned company, grown from Ed Sabol's film business, that films pro football

look.title: Two Ways to Remember 1954
look.text: Fan A watched Game 1 of the 1954 World Series from the Polo Grounds bleachers. She saw ten innings, a tie, a famous catch, and a pinch-hit home run that won it. Fan B was born in 1990. He has seen Willie Mays's catch many times on video. He has never seen or read about the home run.
look.prompt: What does each fan know about the game, and which memory is more complete?

check.q: Who won Game 1 of the 1954 World Series with a home run?
check.why: Pinch hitter Dusty Rhodes hit a three-run home run in the tenth inning.

check.q: What is collective memory?
choices: what a whole group remembers together about the past
check.why: Collective memory is a group's shared memory, often shaped by the images it sees most.

check.q: How did NFL Films begin?
choices: as Ed Sabol's small company that filmed the 1962 NFL championship
as a newspaper in St. Louis
check.why: Ed Sabol's company filmed the 1962 title game; the NFL bought it in the mid-1960s.

lessons.title: Tapes That Were Lost
lessons.mainIdea: Many early sports broadcasts were never saved, so some famous games survive only in pieces, and memory depends on what was kept.
reading: Early television was mostly live. Videotape was costly, and networks often taped over old programs to reuse the tape. Before videotape, the only way to save a broadcast was a *kinescope*, a film made by pointing a movie camera at a television screen. Many kinescopes were thrown away because no one expected to need them.

Game 7 of the 1960 World Series ended with Bill Mazeroski's home run for the Pittsburgh Pirates against the New York Yankees. For decades, no complete broadcast was known to exist. In 2009, a full kinescope was found in the wine cellar of singer Bing Crosby, who had been a part owner of the Pirates. Crosby had asked for a film of the game.

Super Bowl I was carried by two networks in 1967, yet neither is known to have kept a complete tape. Fans and researchers have pieced it together from partial recordings. These gaps matter to historians. An *archive* is a place where records are saved and cared for. When the archive is empty, later generations know a game only through the pieces that survived.

words.d: a film made by recording a television screen, used to save early broadcasts
a place or collection where records and recordings are saved and cared for
to record a new program on a used tape, erasing what was there

look.title: A Film in a Wine Cellar

look.prompt: What does this case show about how luck can decide which parts of sport history survive?
